title: Draining of the Mesopotamian marshes and displacement of the Maʿdān
summary: After the failed 1991 uprising in southern Iraq, the government turned a limited drainage scheme into a systematic effort to dry the marshes at the Tigris–Euphrates confluence. Satellite images showed the wetlands had lost most of their area by 2000. The Maʿdān, or Marsh Arabs, about 250,000 in 1991, were killed, expelled or made refugees, with under 40,000 left in their homeland by 2003.

uncertainty.note: Draining began in the late 1980s as a limited scheme and became systematic after 1991 (RFE/RL). The end year is the date HRW described the campaign as ongoing (January 2003); reflooding is placed only in "the early 2000s" by UNESCO.

as_recorded.value: a deliberate policy by Baghdad since 1991
Starting shortly after the end of the Gulf war in 1991

where.modern_name: Mesopotamian Marshes (al-Ahwar), southern Iraq; pin at Hawr al-Hammar
where.historical_name: Marshes (ahwar) of southern Iraq around the Tigris–Euphrates confluence, under Baʿathist Iraq

importance.justification: A state-driven ecological disaster that destroyed one of the world's largest wetlands and the home of an ancient community.

audience_note: Concerns state violence against the Maʿdān, including killings, arrests and forced displacement.
